services.name: Drain Cleaning
services.title: Drain Cleaning | LK Plumbing Company Leander | Leander, TX
services.meta: LK Plumbing Company Leander handles slow, backed-up, and odorous drains in Leander, TX. We inspect the line, clear blockages, and explain next steps.
services.blurb: We clear slow, backed-up drains across Leander and nearby communities.

paragraphs: A kitchen sink that gurgles after the tap stops, a shower that holds water at your feet, or a sour odor from a floor drain usually starts the call. We trace those signs through the trap, branch pipe, and accessible cleanout instead of treating the smell alone. Food residue, soap film, hair, and paper can narrow different sections of the line and change how water leaves the fixture.

Water may drain slowly in one bathroom while a nearby tub bubbles because both fixtures meet at the same branch. We work on drain blockages in Leander, Cedar Park, Jonestown, and Liberty Hill from our S West Dr location, checking the fixture that shows the symptom and the route beyond it. A wet ring under a sink or water rising in a shower while another fixture empties gives us a useful starting point.

A single slow sink can sometimes wait while you limit use and watch its water level. A drain that sends wastewater into a tub, shower, or floor drain should not wait, because the blockage can force water out of the branch pipe and onto flooring, cabinets, or drywall.

sections.heading: Gurgling sinks and sewer smells
paragraphs: Customers often say, "my sink gurgles," "the shower will not drain," or "a sewer smell comes up after we run water." We also hear that the kitchen sink backs up into the other bowl, the toilet flush makes bubbles in the tub, or the laundry standpipe spills onto the floor. A clog near a fixture, a blocked branch, and a restriction farther along the line can produce similar sounds and water levels. We inspect before choosing a tool because those faults call for different access points and different amounts of work, even though they can sound identical over the phone.

sections.heading: Drain line inspection
paragraphs: During a drain line inspection, we begin at the affected sink, tub, shower, or floor drain and run water to watch the flow and listen for air movement. We check the trap, visible pipe joints, and available cleanout, then note the pipe diameter, the water level, and how far a cable can travel before meeting resistance. An accessible fixture check and cleanout test often take 20 to 40 minutes, while a cable that must pass farther through a branch line takes longer to clear and test.

We can often remove hair, soap buildup, food residue, or paper from an accessible drain on the same visit. If a trap washer leaks after removal, a cleanout cap has seized, or camera footage points to a damaged section of pipe, we explain the next repair before booking further work. Opening a wall, replacing a buried pipe section, or arranging access to a shared line may need a separate visit.

sections.heading: Cleanout access and pipe route
paragraphs: An exposed cleanout beside the house, in a garage, or beneath a sink usually gives us a direct route to the blockage. A drain line hidden behind a cabinet, below a slab, or beyond a fixture trap can require more setup and a different cable path. Older cast-iron pipe, root intrusion, heavy grease buildup, and repeated backups can also change the work needed to restore flow.

A removable trap lets us inspect the first section of pipe without disturbing a countertop or cabinet base. If the blockage sits farther down the route, we may need to use another cleanout or inspect the line with a camera before deciding whether cleaning alone will hold. Work that moves beyond the drain line and into walls, flooring, or a shared building connection can also require owner approval or sign-off.

sections.heading: Fixture and cleanout location
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room has the slow drain and which fixture causes another fixture to gurgle or back up. Tell us whether water is standing in the sink, tub, shower, or floor drain right now, and whether the blockage affects one fixture or several. If you can safely see a cleanout cap, let us know whether it sits outside, in a garage, under a sink, or behind an access panel.

Visible pipe material, such as PVC, ABS, or cast iron, can help us plan the right cable head and fittings. Let us know if a cabinet, parked vehicle, locked gate, or crawlspace blocks access to the cleanout. Call LK Plumbing Company Leander at (512) 563-3818 before a slow drain turns into wastewater backing up through a tub, shower, or floor drain.

services.name: Water Heater Repair
services.h1: Water Heater Repair in Leander, TX
services.title: Heater Repair - LK Plumbing Company Leander, Leander, TX
services.meta: LK Plumbing Company Leander handles water heater repair in Leander, TX, for cold water, leaks, pilot faults, elements, valves, and tank checks, 1000 S West Dr.
services.blurb: We repair leaking, cold, noisy, and unreliable water heaters in Leander.

paragraphs: Cold water at every hot tap and water spreading from the base of a heater often get called the same problem, but they point to different repairs. A hallway may reveal a puddle near the utility closet, while a shower may run cold with no water visible at the tank. We handle both a heater that has stopped heating and a heater that is releasing water from a valve, fitting, or tank.

We work from 1000 S West Dr and cover Leander, Cedar Park, Jonestown, and Liberty Hill. A heater producing only cold water can sometimes wait briefly while the source is checked, but water on the floor should not wait because a leaking tank or relief valve can damage flooring, framing, and nearby electrical connections.

sections.heading: No hot water and puddles
paragraphs: Customers often report “no hot water,” “hot water runs out fast,” “water around the heater,” or “the pilot will not stay lit.” An electric heater may lose heat through an element, thermostat, high-limit switch, or wiring connection. A gas heater with a pilot that drops out can involve the thermocouple, igniter, burner assembly, or gas control valve.

Popping or rumbling from the tank can come from sediment under the lower element or burner area, while rusty water may point toward corrosion inside the tank or a worn anode rod. Water at the heater may come from the temperature-pressure relief valve, a supply fitting, the drain valve, or the tank shell itself. These symptoms can look alike from the kitchen or hallway, but the failed part and the labor needed to reach it can lead to very different repair work.

sections.heading: Heater inspection and test
paragraphs: We begin the inspection at the heater, checking the model plate, fuel type, visible piping, shutoff valve, drain valve, vent connection, and floor around the base. We check for moisture at fittings before testing heat, then measure incoming water pressure; most residential plumbing runs within a range of about 40 to 80 psi. For electric units, we isolate power before testing elements, thermostats, and wiring, while gas units require checks of the pilot, burner flame, ignition sequence, and venting. A straightforward diagnostic inspection commonly takes 30 to 60 minutes, depending on access and the fault.

We can often replace a thermostat, heating element, thermocouple, relief valve, or accessible supply fitting during the same visit when the correct part is available. We test the heater after the repair and compare the outlet temperature with the control setting; 120 degrees Fahrenheit is a common household setting. A tank with a failed shell, inaccessible vent work, or a part that must be ordered may require a return visit or separate replacement work.

sections.heading: Anode rods and shutoffs
paragraphs: Tank age and the condition of the anode rod can change the scope of a repair. A heater with an accessible element panel or relief valve usually takes less strip-back than one set in a tight closet behind shelving, ductwork, or a finished wall. Corrosion around the tank seam can also shift the work away from a replaceable fitting and toward tank replacement.

A seized cold-water shutoff adds labor because we may need to address the valve before isolating the heater safely. A manufacturer-specific gas control, electronic board, or tankless component may need to be ordered rather than fitted from common stock. Permit or inspection sign-off, where required for replacement or vent changes, also affects the work planned for the heater.

sections.heading: Model plate and closet access
paragraphs: Before calling, check the manufacturer data plate on the heater and have the model and serial number available. The plate may sit on the side of the tank, behind a removable panel, or near the burner compartment. If you know the approximate installation age, tell us that along with whether the unit uses gas or electricity.

Let us know which room holds the heater, whether water is running from the base or a valve, and whether the closet, attic, or garage access has a clear path. A photo of the pipes above the heater and the floor below it can help us identify the likely fitting and bring suitable parts. Call LK Plumbing Company Leander at (512) 563-3818 before a tank leak spreads into the wall, floor, or framing.

services.name: Toilet Repair
services.title: Toilet Repair | LK Plumbing Company Leander | Leander, TX
services.meta: LK Plumbing Company Leander handles toilet repairs in Leander, TX, checking tanks, fill valves, flappers, shutoff valves, leaks, and loose bases.
services.blurb: Running toilets, leaks, weak flushes, and loose toilet repairs in Leander.

paragraphs: A toilet that refills every few minutes can waste water for a week before the sound becomes hard to ignore. Over a month, a worn flapper or fill valve can keep the tank cycling long after the bathroom is empty, and a water meter may continue moving even with every faucet off. We trace the refill cycle at the tank so the water loss does not keep building behind a closed door.

Water around the base causes a different kind of damage. A loose closet bolt, failed wax ring, or hairline crack can let each flush wet the flooring beneath the bowl, where moisture can soften subflooring and stain the ceiling below. We check the base, tank, supply line, and shutoff valve before replacing a part that may not be causing the leak.

A handle that sticks or a toilet that needs an extra flush may allow a short delay if the bowl stays stable and no water reaches the floor. Recurring running, leaking, rocking, or overflowing should not wait, because each flush can send more water through a failed seal, valve, or connection.

sections.heading: Toilet keeps running
paragraphs: We hear several versions of the same call: the toilet keeps running, the tank will not fill, the handle does nothing, or water leaks around the bottom of the toilet. A tank that hisses after flushing often points to a fill valve or flapper, while a tank that fills slowly can involve the shutoff valve, supply tube, or mineral buildup at the valve inlet. A weak flush can come from a low tank water level, a loose lift chain, or clogged rim holes under the bowl edge.

A toilet that rocks under weight, leaves water at the base, or sends the bowl level upward after flushing needs a different inspection than a noisy tank. We also check a toilet that flushes by itself, because water can slip past the flapper without leaving a puddle. Similar sounds and puddles can hide very different failed parts, so the labor and replacement parts depend on what we find at the fixture.

sections.heading: Tank and bowl inspection
paragraphs: We start at the shutoff valve and supply tube, then remove the tank lid and flush the bowl while watching the flapper, chain, overflow tube, fill valve, and tank water level. A refill and dye check commonly takes 10 to 20 minutes, while a leak at the base may require several flushes and a closer look at the closet bolts. We can also test water pressure at the nearby supply line; residential plumbing commonly operates within a 40 to 80 psi range.

We replace standard flappers, fill valves, handles, tank bolts, supply tubes, and shutoff valves during the same visit when the matching part is available and the toilet does not need removal. A cracked bowl, damaged flange, seized valve connection, or toilet that needs replacement can require a follow-up visit for the correct fixture, parts, and access work. If a blockage sits beyond the toilet trapway, we explain that before any separate drain work begins.

sections.heading: Shutoff valve and tank parts
paragraphs: The part inside the tank changes the scope of a repair. A flapper or lift chain usually allows direct access under the tank lid, while a corroded tank bolt, split overflow tube, or damaged fill valve can require more disassembly and careful handling of porcelain. Older toilets may also use discontinued flush valves or nonstandard handle assemblies that need matching parts.

Access at the shutoff valve matters as much as the tank hardware. A valve that turns freely lets us isolate the toilet before working on the supply tube, but a seized valve, corroded compression nut, or tight wall opening adds work around the water line. We also account for a loose bowl, a failed wax ring, flooring around the base, and any replacement part that must be ordered before we can finish the repair.

sections.heading: Tank model and bathroom
paragraphs: Before calling, check which bathroom holds the toilet and whether water is running into the bowl or onto the floor now. We can use the brand name and model marking from inside the tank, beneath the tank lid, or on the porcelain to bring a closer match for the flapper, handle, or fill valve.

Note whether the bowl rocks, the handle sticks, the tank refills on its own, or the flush sends water toward the rim. Tell us if the shutoff valve sits behind the bowl, inside a cabinet opening, or near finished flooring, since that access affects the valve work. A photo of the tank interior and the supply connection can help us identify the parts before the visit. Call LK Plumbing Company Leander at (512) 563-3818 before a running tank wastes more water or a base leak reaches the flooring.

services.name: Pipe Leak Repair
services.h1: Pipe Leak Repair in Leander, TX
services.title: Pipe Leak Repair | LK Plumbing Company Leander, Leander, TX
services.meta: LK Plumbing Company Leander repairs pipe leaks in Leander, TX. We trace wet walls, ceiling stains, and hidden water lines, then explain repair work.
services.blurb: We trace and repair pipe leaks before water reaches walls, cabinets, and ceilings.

paragraphs: Most people start by closing the angle stop beneath a sink, turning off a fixture valve, or setting a bucket under the drip. That is a sensible first move because it can keep water off cabinet flooring while we trace the source. The approach stops helping when water comes from a wall, ceiling, slab edge, or a pipe joint that remains pressurized after the fixture valve closes. A towel catches visible water, but it cannot dry the cavity behind drywall.

We treat an active pipe leak as work that should not wait, especially when water reaches a ceiling, wall plate, cabinet base, or electrical outlet. Even a slow leak can soak insulation and drywall long after the floor looks dry. A loose connection under an open sink may allow time for a planned repair, but water inside a wall or ceiling needs attention before the wet area spreads.

sections.heading: Water stain and hissing
paragraphs: Customers often call about a brown ceiling spot, a hissing sound behind a wall, water pooling beneath a cabinet, or a water meter that keeps moving after faucets and appliances are off. Some find paint bubbling near a baseboard, while others notice a warm section of floor or a musty smell in a closet. A dripping copper joint, a split PEX line, a failed compression fitting, and a leak under a slab can look alike from the room side. We inspect the pipe route because those faults need different repairs and involve different materials, access, and labor.

sections.heading: Leak inspection
paragraphs: We begin by checking the visible pipe, fixture shutoff, meter movement, and moisture around the affected wall or cabinet. We may isolate a branch line, read water pressure, and listen at the pipe route before opening drywall. A visible supply connection can often be inspected within twenty to forty minutes, while a hidden leak takes longer to narrow down without removing unnecessary material.

On the same visit, we can often replace an exposed PEX fitting, copper coupling, valve connection, or short damaged section of pipe. We shut off the water, remove the failed fitting, install compatible material, and test the repaired line under pressure before restoring service. A leak beneath tile, inside a structural wall, or along a slab route may require a separate visit for access work, pipe rerouting, or an inspection sign-off.

sections.heading: Shutoffs, walls, and pipe material
paragraphs: Pipe material changes the repair work because copper, PEX, CPVC, galvanized steel, and PVC use different fittings, cutting tools, and connection methods. An exposed PEX coupling inside a sink cabinet usually gives us direct access, while an older threaded pipe behind plaster can require more careful removal. The age of the fitting also matters when corrosion has spread beyond the first wet joint.

A seized house shutoff can add work before we can safely isolate the leaking line. Drywall, tile, cabinets, insulation, and a pipe route inside a ceiling can all affect how much access we need to create and restore. If a valve, specialty fitting, or matching pipe material must be ordered, or if the repair needs an inspection sign-off, we explain that before scheduling the next part of the work.

sections.heading: Pipe material and access panel
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room has the leak and whether it sits beneath a sink, behind a refrigerator, near a washing machine, or above a ceiling fixture. If you can see the pipe, tell us whether it appears to be copper, white or tan plastic, gray plastic, or flexible PEX tubing. For a leak near a pressure regulator, filtration housing, or manifold, read the model number from the label or plate if it remains dry and accessible.

Let us know whether water is still running, whether the house shutoff works, and whether an access panel, cabinet back, crawl space, or attic reaches the pipe. Photos of the stain, wet cabinet floor, exposed fitting, or access opening can help us plan the right fittings and tools. Call LK Plumbing Company Leander at (512) 563-3818 before wet drywall, insulation, or a ceiling cavity absorbs more water.

services.name: Faucet Repair
services.title: Faucet Repair | LK Plumbing Company Leander, Leander, TX
services.meta: LK Plumbing Company Leander handles faucet repair in Leander, TX, checking drips, handles, cartridges, valves, and under-sink shutoffs at the fixture.
services.blurb: We track down drips, loose handles, low flow, and valve faults at kitchen and bath faucets.

paragraphs: Calls about a faucet often start with, “It keeps dripping,” “the handle just spins,” or “hardly any water comes out.” We translate those descriptions into a check of the handle, cartridge, spout, aerator, supply lines, and shutoff valves beneath the sink. A kitchen faucet and a bathroom faucet can make the same sound while failing at different parts.

We also hear about water collecting around the faucet base, a handle that takes both hands to move, or a stream that sprays sideways into the sink. Mineral buildup can restrict an aerator, while a worn cartridge can let water pass after the handle closes. A slow drip can usually wait for planned repair, but a faucet that will not shut off or sends water into the cabinet should not wait because water can soak the sink base and keep running through the meter.

sections.heading: Dripping tap and loose handle
paragraphs: A steady drip from the spout after the handle closes often points to a worn cartridge, stem seal, washer, or valve seat. A faucet that squeals, chatters, or bangs as water flows can involve a loose washer, restricted aerator, or pressure movement in the supply line. Low flow from one faucet, while the rest of the house has normal flow, commonly starts at the aerator or cartridge rather than the main water line.

A handle that turns without changing the water, pulls away from the faucet body, or becomes hard to move can have a stripped adapter, loose set screw, corroded stem, or seized cartridge. Water appearing at the base of the spout can come from O-rings inside the faucet rather than from the countertop seal. These symptoms can look alike from above the sink, but the failed part, access under the fixture, and required repair can lead to different work and different costs.

sections.heading: Sink valve inspection
paragraphs: We start at the faucet body, run both hot and cold water, and watch the spout, handle, spray hose, and base for leaks. We remove the aerator where needed, check for debris, and test the shutoff valves under the sink before taking the faucet apart. We can also measure water pressure at the fixture; residential pressure commonly falls between 40 and 80 psi, although a restricted faucet can show poor flow even within that range.

A straightforward aerator cleaning, handle repair, cartridge replacement, or O-ring change can often be completed during the same visit when the correct part is available and the shutoffs operate. An inspection and basic disassembly commonly take 20 to 40 minutes, while corrosion, a seized retaining nut, or a concealed faucet mounting bracket can add time. We book a return visit when a cartridge, valve stem, specialty hose, or manufacturer-specific part has to be ordered, or when cabinet access requires more extensive work.

sections.heading: Seized shutoffs and cartridge access
paragraphs: The age of the faucet matters because older cartridges, stems, and retaining clips may no longer match current replacement parts. A common faucet with an accessible cartridge beneath the handle generally involves less work than a discontinued model with a specialty valve body. The make stamped on the spout or handle can help us determine whether a repair part remains available.

Access under the sink also changes the work. A shutoff valve that turns freely lets us isolate the faucet, while a seized, corroded, or leaking shutoff can require additional attention before we can remove the cartridge or supply hose. Tight cabinets, a garbage disposal beside the water lines, damaged mounting hardware, and an ordered part can each move the repair toward a longer or return visit.

sections.heading: Model number and faucet plate
paragraphs: Before calling, check which room holds the faucet and whether it serves a kitchen sink, bathroom sink, bar sink, or utility sink. Look for the brand name on the spout, handle, escutcheon plate, or installation papers, and keep any model number from the box or receipt nearby. Tell us whether water drips from the spout, escapes around the handle, leaks into the cabinet, or runs continuously.

We also need to know whether the hot and cold shutoff valves sit within reach under the sink and whether a disposal, pullout hose, or stored items block the cabinet. A photo of the faucet and the space beneath the sink can help identify the cartridge style and mounting arrangement before we arrive. Call LK Plumbing Company Leander at (512) 563-3818 before a continuing drip wears the cartridge or valve seat further and sends more water through the faucet.

services.name: Garbage Disposal Repair
services.h1: Garbage Disposal Repair in Leander, TX
services.title: LK Plumbing Company Leander | Leander, TX Disposal
services.meta: LK Plumbing Company Leander handles garbage disposal repair in Leander, TX, checking humming motors, leaks, switches, mounting rings, and sink drains.
services.blurb: We repair humming, leaking, jammed, and non-working garbage disposals.

paragraphs: Older single-family kitchens in Leander, Cedar Park, Jonestown, and Liberty Hill often have a disposal that has worked through years of food scraps, detergent, and hard-water buildup beneath the sink. The motor, mounting ring, splash guard, and dishwasher drain connection all sit inside a tight sink cabinet, where a small leak or loose fitting can go unnoticed until water reaches the cabinet floor. We check the disposal and its connections before treating a humming unit as a motor failure.

A disposal can stop after a jam, a tripped reset button, a failed wall switch, or a worn motor. Water under the sink may come from the disposal housing, the mounting assembly, the dishwasher hose, or the trap beside it. A disposal that hums, leaks, smells hot, or trips a breaker should not keep running or receive repeated reset attempts, because a seized motor, damaged wiring, or loose mounting ring can worsen while the unit stays in use.

sections.heading: Humming sink and food odor
paragraphs: Customers often call because the disposal hums but the grinding plate will not turn, or because the switch does nothing and the sink fills with food scraps. A rotten food odor can come up through the splash guard even after the basin has been cleaned, especially when debris remains around the grinding chamber. Water may drip from the bottom of the disposal, run down the side of the housing, or collect beneath the mounting ring where the unit meets the sink. These symptoms can look similar from the kitchen counter, but a jammed impeller, failed motor, worn seal, blocked outlet, and loose mount each call for different parts and different work.

sections.heading: Under-sink disposal inspection
paragraphs: We start by shutting off power at the breaker, then inspect the cord or hardwired connection, wall switch, reset button, splash guard, mounting ring, and drain outlet. A meter check can confirm whether the disposal receives the expected 120-volt power supply, while a manual inspection helps identify a jammed grinding plate or foreign object in the chamber. We also check the 1 1/2-inch drain connection, trap, and dishwasher hose for water escaping into the cabinet.

A basic inspection and functional test commonly takes about 20 to 40 minutes, depending on cabinet access and whether water has reached the electrical connection. We can often clear a jam, reset the unit, tighten a mounting assembly, or replace a failed switch component during the same visit when the needed part matches the disposal. A replacement disposal, uncommon mounting part, or damaged electrical connection may need a return visit after the correct model or component has been obtained.

sections.heading: Motor, mounting ring, cabinet access
paragraphs: The disposal motor and the condition of the mounting ring move the scope of repair more than a visible drip alone suggests. An older unit with a leaking lower seal may need replacement rather than a small adjustment, while a loose mount or worn splash guard may involve less disassembly. Tight cabinet space, a built-in water filter, stored cleaning supplies, or a dishwasher hose routed across the disposal can add time before we can reach the housing and wiring. If the exact motor, sink flange, or mounting assembly must be ordered, or a rental property needs owner approval before replacement, the work may require a separate return visit.

sections.heading: Model plate and sink cabinet
paragraphs: Before calling, check the disposal model number on the label attached to the side or bottom of the housing. Note whether the unit has stopped completely, hums at the switch, leaks from the bottom, or backs water into the sink. Let us know which kitchen sink has the disposal and whether a dishwasher drain hose connects to it. If possible, clear bottles and supplies from the sink cabinet so we can reach the outlet, reset button, and mounting ring. Call LK Plumbing Company Leander at (512) 563-3818 before a leak from the disposal housing damages the cabinet base or reaches the electrical connection.
